variation.original_summary: Turn The Tide is a 3-5 player card game. Each hand, everyone plays a numbered Weather card at the same moment. The two highest cards are forced to take one of two revealed Tide Level cards, and whoever then shows the highest Tide loses a life preserver. Hands pass around the table over as many rounds as there are players, and the score is preservers kept, minus a penalty for elimination, plus a bonus for the lowest Tide.

review.evidence: The core is sound. All cards are played at once and no seat has an edge, and hand passing evens out the deal. The tested variation had a hole, though. Everyone started at Tide 11, the median of a 1-20 Tide deck. In 4-player games a player who always plays their lowest card often stays at 11 while others capture High Tides averaging about 14, so pure passivity bled few lifelines. Sunk players also still counted toward 'highest Tide' while losing nothing, so they shielded everyone else.

Every player plays every original hand once, so luck of the deal cancels out over the game. What separates players is when they spend high cards, reading the two revealed Tides, and predicting which cards rivals will commit. All of these can be learned.

A weak player still keeps some lifelines and can earn the lowest-Tide bonus. A strong player can count which cards are public, track which cards each opponent still holds, and time sacrifices across 10 hands. The game is not solved.

In deal 1 the hands are hidden, so inference matters. In the tested variation every card was eventually played, so from deal 2 on every hand was fully public and the residual uncertainty was only what rivals will choose. Opponent modelling still matters, but the hidden-information component was thin.
Card comparisons, Tide levels, lifeline losses and end-of-deal scoring are all integer arithmetic on tracked numbers.

The tested variation broke at round 11. Played cards were discarded, so the hands to pass were empty and the stated 'each hand played once' rule was impossible. The 10th hand of each deal was also a forced play with one card left. Otherwise it was turn-based, text-only and within limits.

variation.name: Turn The Tide: Short Seas (revised)
variation.summary: This is a 3-4 player Turn The Tide over P deals of 10 hands. Players hold 11 numbered Weather cards and play one per hand at the same moment. The two highest plays must take the two revealed Tide cards, and whoever is highest on the Tide loses a lifeline. Hands rotate left so everyone plays every hand once, and one card of each hand always stays hidden from rivals.
variation.rules:
SETUP. Let P be the number of players (3 or 4). The Weather deck is the cards 1 to 12xP (1-36 for 3 players, 1-48 for 4), each number once. Shuffle it and deal 11 cards face down to each player as that player's hand. The remaining P cards are set aside face down and stay unseen for the whole game. Each player starts with a game score of 0. The game has P deals of 10 hands each, so 10xP hands in total. One round is one hand.

INFORMATION. You always see your own hand. Every Weather card becomes public the moment it is played and stays face up in front of whoever played it until the end of that deal. Unplayed cards and set-aside cards are never shown. So from deal 2 on, every player knows the cards of a passed hand that were played in earlier deals but not its unplayed card or cards, unless they held that hand themselves.

START OF EACH DEAL (before hand 1 of deals 1 to P):
- Shuffle a Tide deck of the cards 1 to 20.
- Set every player's Tide level to 15.
- Give every player 4 lifelines.
- Clear every player's Sunk status.
- From deal 2 on: each player takes all 10 Weather cards lying face up in front of them, plus the 1 card still in their hand, making 11 cards. They pass these 11 cards as a hand to the player on their left. The face-up rows are now empty. Over the P deals each player plays each of the P original hands exactly once.

EACH HAND (10 per deal):
1. Reveal the next two cards of the Tide deck to everyone. The smaller is Low Tide and the larger is High Tide.
2. Every player secretly chooses one Weather card from their hand. All choices are revealed at the same time and each card is placed face up in front of the player who played it.
3. The player who played the highest Weather card sets their Tide level to Low Tide. The player who played the second highest sets their Tide level to High Tide. All others keep their current Tide level. Weather numbers are unique, so there are no ties. Sunk players take part in this step like anyone else.
4. Among players who are NOT Sunk, find the highest Tide level. Every non-Sunk player at that level loses 1 lifeline. A player who must lose a lifeline while at 0 lifelines becomes Sunk instead. A Sunk player stays Sunk until the next deal, keeps playing cards and is ignored in this step. If every player is Sunk, nothing happens.
5. Announce all Weather cards played, all Tide levels, all lifelines and all Sunk statuses.

END OF EACH DEAL (after hand 10 of each deal), adjust each game score:
- Each player who is not Sunk adds their remaining lifelines (0 to 4).
- Each Sunk player subtracts 1.
- Among players who are not Sunk, the player or players with the lowest Tide level each add 1.
After each deal every player holds exactly 1 card, which is not shown to others.

There is no talk phase.

END. After deal P, the game ends and the winner is decided as in the objective.
variation.objective: After the last deal, the player with the highest game score wins. If several players tie for the highest score, the tied player with the lowest Tide level at the end of the last deal wins. If that is still tied, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: The fixed hand-passing makes every deal playable. Each player meets each original hand once, so the deal is not a lottery. Starting at Tide 15 makes passivity costly: a player who hoards high cards and dumps low ones stays at 15 and bleeds lifelines. Burning high cards early instead leaves you unable to escape a bad High Tide later. Skill means deciding when a pair of Tides is worth spending a high card on, forcing rivals into the second-highest slot, and predicting their cards from the public record and the one hidden card per hand. Ignoring Sunk players keeps pressure on the live players to the end of each deal. Talk is left out: it cannot bind, and promises about card timing in a game where only one player wins would be empty or simply ignored.

balanced.evidence: Main decision: which Weather card to play after the two Tide cards are seen. Outcomes for one hand, where L and H are the revealed Tide cards and T is a player's kept level: highest Weather goes to L, which is usually safe; second highest goes to H, which is the danger; every other player keeps T. The highest level loses 1 lifeline. Distribution of H, the larger of two cards drawn from 1-20: P(H<11) = C(10,2)/C(20,2) = 45/190 = 0.24; P(H=11) = 10/190 = 0.05; P(H>11) = 0.71; E[H] is about 14 and E[L] about 7. Thoughtless policies, checked against the winner rule: (a) ALWAYS LOWEST, 3 players. While you stay out of the top two you keep level 11. You hold or share the maximum only when H<=11, about 29% of hands, so you lose about 2.9 lifelines per 10 hands. The holder of H loses about 71% of hands, a load the two others share, about 35% each. That is slightly better than average early. But the policy plays your hand in ascending order, so late in the deal you are forced to play your highest cards. You then take Low or High Tide at random, and you get no control over the lowest-Tide bonus. An opponent who keeps one high card for the last hand takes the bonus. The policy loses to sensible play and wins only some games against random play. (b) ALWAYS HIGHEST. You take L early and are then stuck at whatever level you last held while your low cards lose. Opponents who keep mid-high cards for the last hands decide the bonus, and they can push H onto you whenever you play your last high card in a high-tide hand. Not dominant. (c) Highest card when H is large, lowest card otherwise: this is just sensible play, and it depends on what opponents still hold. No option is strictly better whatever opponents do, because the second-highest seat is bad while first is good and their order depends on everyone's cards. Choices are simultaneous and seats are symmetric, so there is no move-order edge. Rotating hands (once repaired, see playable) removes the edge from the deal. Every player can realistically win. Scoring is consistent: lifelines 0-4, Sunk -1 against 0 lifelines 0, and +1 for lowest Tide.

playable.evidence: Fatal rule contradiction. Each deal has 10 hands, each player holds 10 cards, and every played card is 'discarded face up'. So after round 10 every hand is empty. The rule 'each player passes their entire current hand of 10 cards to the left' then passes nothing, and deals 2 to P cannot be played. The claim 'Each player plays each original hand exactly once' is impossible under the stated discard rule; the original game returns played cards to the hand before passing. A model with only these words cannot play round 11. The rest is acceptable. Complexity is within limits: rounds 30/40 <= 40, steps 10, choice steps 1, attributes 11, hidden elements 2-3. The Tide deck of 20 is used exactly over 10 hands of 2 reveals. Scoring is arithmetic, and Sunk and tie handling is defined. The lack of talk is acceptable: with 3-4 players the information that matters (cards played, levels, lifelines) is public each hand, so players can infer and model each other rather than guess, and talk could not bind. Minor point: the 10th hand of each deal is forced, since only one card is left, which is wasted but harmless.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: Hidden information: the opponents' hands in deal 1 and the 2P set-aside cards. Played cards are public, so players can count cards and infer which high cards opponents still hold. The Tide reveals are public before each choice, so the decision is about timing. Choose when to spend high cards (to take L), avoid being second highest (taking H), and keep a high card for the last hands to claim the lowest-Tide bonus. All of this depends on predicting the opponents' cards. Once hands are recycled and rotated, every player plays every hand exactly once, so deal luck balances out. From deal 2 on, all holdings are known, because each hand was fully revealed when played, and the game becomes pure simultaneous-move opponent modelling. Chance remains in the Tide order, which differs per deal, and in deal-1 card strength. I estimate chance at about 25-35% of the result. When all players play well, the outcome is decided by timing and reading of opponents, not by the draw alone. A good reasoner should clearly beat a thoughtless policy. This assessment depends on fixing the hand-recycling rule; without it, the deal-1 hand decides much more.

required_changes: Replace 'those cards are discarded face up' with: played Weather cards are placed face up in front of the player who played them. At END OF EACH DEAL each player picks up their own 10 played cards as their hand, and it is this hand that is passed to the left before the next deal. This makes 'each player plays each original hand exactly once' true.

State explicitly that because all cards are revealed when played, every player knows every hand from deal 2 onward. This is acceptable and intended, but the rules should not imply that hands remain hidden.

Optional: say that 'START OF EACH DEAL (rounds 1, 11, 21, 31)' means the deals that exist, so rounds 1, 11 and 21 for 3 players. Also consider dealing 11 cards for 10 hands, so the final hand of each deal is a real choice.

balanced.evidence:
The game is symmetric. All choices are simultaneous, and over P deals each player plays each of the P original hands exactly once, so seat order and deal quality even out. The key decision: winning a hand gives you Low Tide, finishing second forces High Tide on you, and anyone else KEEPS their level, which no opponent can change. Tide values: for two cards from 1-20, E[Low] is about 7 and E[High] is about 14. P(High > 15) = 1 - C(15,2)/C(20,2) = 1 - 105/190, about 0.45. The deck has 20 cards and 10 hands x 2 = 20, so it is used exactly.

Thoughtless policies against the winner rule:
(a) Always lowest card. You never take a tide, since you are third or fourth every hand, so you sit at 15. Opponents mostly hold Low Tides (about 7) or sometimes High Tides below 15, so you are often the highest non-Sunk player. You take about 5 or more of the 10 losses, sink, and score -1 per deal. You lose to sensible play and usually to random play.
(b) Always highest card. You win the early hands with an 11-card hand dealt from 36 or 48 cards. Once your top cards are gone, your 'highest remaining' often comes second and forces High Tide on you. Meanwhile a sensible player holds back a high card for a late hand where the remaining Tide cards (countable, because all 20 are known) include a very low value. That player takes the last-deal lowest-Tide bonus and avoids the losses. Always-highest beats random play often but loses to sensible play, so it does not 'never lose'.
(c) Always first or last listed card: equivalent to random play, so it loses to sensible play.
(d) The 'freeze' line: win once with a low Low Tide, then dump low cards. This is strong but beatable. In a 3-player game, dumping can still leave you second and force High Tide on you, so you must model what opponents will play.

No option is strictly better whatever the opponents do. All players can realistically win. Score range per deal is -1 to 5, decided by lifelines plus the lowest-Tide bonus. The labelled payoffs are consistent with the description.

playable.evidence:
The rules are complete and deterministic:
- Ties for highest Weather card are impossible, because the numbers are unique.
- Ties for highest Tide are handled: all players at that level lose a lifeline.
- Sunk at 0 lifelines is defined, and every-player-Sunk is handled.
- The card count works. Each player has 11 cards and plays 10, then 10 face-up cards plus 1 in hand = 11 are passed left, so each original hand is played once by each player.
- Starting Tide 15 can collide with a drawn 15. The lowest-Tide bonus and the tiebreak handle ties.
- The game is finite: 10xP hands, which is 30 or 40.
- The winner is decided by arithmetic on recorded scores and Tide levels.

Complexity against the platform limits:
- steps 13 against a limit of 20;
- choice steps 1 against 4;
- attributes 12 against 20;
- hidden elements 3 against 3 (own hand, unplayed card, set-aside cards);
- random draws 1 against 1 (one Tide shuffle per deal; the reveals are list removals);
- rounds 40 against 40 for P = 4, which is at the limit but allowed.

It needs no board, clock or judge. Leaving out talk is defensible. Interests conflict, but talk would not bind, and the strategic content is reading the public card rows, counting the remaining Tide cards and predicting simultaneous plays. Players are not reduced to blind guessing, because all played cards and the passed-hand history are public.

Minor gap: the final tiebreak does not say whether Sunk players' Tide levels count. This is worth clarifying but not blocking.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
There is real inference.
- Tide counting: the deck composition 1-20 is known, and each reveal narrows what remains. This tells you when to spend high cards.
- Hand tracking: from deal 2 on, you know all played cards of the hand you receive, and of the hands opponents hold, except 1 to 3 hidden cards. You can estimate opponents' remaining high cards.
- Opponent modelling: you must predict whether you will finish first, second or lower, because second place forces High Tide on you.

Chance comes from the Tide reveal order and the initial deal. The hand rotation cancels most of the deal luck, and the Tide order is shared by all players, so it does not systematically favour anyone. I estimate chance at roughly 25-35% of outcomes.

When all players play well, the winner is decided by timing and reading, not by a hidden type or a single draw. A reasoning player who saves a high card for a low late tide, and avoids second place, clearly beats an always-highest or random player.
